etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) to resolve (a contest, problem, dispute, etc.); to choose, determine, or settle

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: The quarrel toucheth none but us alone; / Betwixt ourselves let us decide it then.

quote.citation: 1987 December 21, Richard Nixon, Letters to Trump, Winning Team Publishing, published 2023, →ISBN, →OCLC, page 10:
quote.text: I did not see the program, but Mrs. Nixon told me that you were great on the Donahue Show.As you can imagine, she is an expert on politics and she predicts that whenever you decide to run for office you will be a winner!

definitions.definition: (intransitive) to make a judgment, especially after deliberation

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Kings 20:40:
quote.text: So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) to cause someone to come to a decision

quote.citation: 1920, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventure of the Three Gables, Norton, published 2005, page 1537:
quote.text: It decides me to look into the matter, for if it is worth anyone's while to take so much trouble, there must be something in it.

quote.citation: 1642, Thomas Fuller, The Holy State, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire:  […]  Roger Daniel for John Williams, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Our seat denies us traffic here; / The sea, too near, decides us from the rest.
